solution:
Compound (2) is an **ether**. It has no \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to one another; its boiling point is close to that of an alkane of comparable molecular mass (Table 11.6 makes exactly this comparison — n-heptane 371 K against methyl n-pentyl ether 373 K, while n-hexyl alcohol of the same molecular mass boils at 430 K). So (2) boils lowest.

Compounds (1) and (3) are both \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) alcohols and both hydrogen-bond, so both boil far above the ether. Between them, branching decides: as branching increases the intermolecular van der Waal's forces weaken and the boiling point falls. (1) is the straight-chain n-butyl alcohol (\(118^\circ\mathrm{C}\), Table 11.5) and (3) is the fully branched tert-butyl alcohol (\(83^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), so (3) boils below (1).

Increasing order is therefore \((2) < (3) < (1)\).

The other three orders each contradict one of these two facts: (A) and (B) put the hydrogen-bonded alcohol (1) below or level with the ether, and (C) puts tert-butyl alcohol below the ether. Only \((2) < (3) < (1)\) is consistent with both.

The substrate is an alkene and the product is an alcohol in which \(\mathrm{-OH}\) sits on the carbon **adjacent** to the methyl-bearing carbon — the less substituted of the two doubly-bonded carbons. That is anti-Markownikoff addition of water, which the chapter obtains by **hydroboration - oxidation**: with diborane \(\mathrm{(B_2H_6)}\) the alkene gives a trialkylborane, and oxidation of that with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline medium gives the alcohol.

Reagent \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\), \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)-\(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is therefore the correct choice.

Ruling the others out: conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)/\(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is acid-catalysed hydration, which follows **Markownikoff's rule** and would put \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on the methyl-bearing carbon instead — the wrong regiochemistry. \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) reduces carbonyl compounds, not isolated \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\), so it leaves the alkene untouched. \(\mathrm{H_2/Pd}\) simply hydrogenates the double bond and introduces no \(\mathrm{-OH}\) at all.

Ethyl alcohol reacts with the active metal sodium to give **sodium ethoxide**, an ionic salt in which the organic fragment is the ethoxide anion:

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + 2\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2}\uparrow\)

The organic product carries a full negative charge, so it is ionic.

Each of the other three gives a **covalent** organic product. With \(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\) and with \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) the alcohol is converted to the alkyl chloride \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Cl}\) (accompanied by \(\mathrm{SO_2}\)/\(\mathrm{HCl}\) and by \(\mathrm{POCl_3}\)/\(\mathrm{HCl}\) respectively) — a neutral covalent molecule. With \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) the alcohol gives alkyl hydrogen sulfate, and on heating an ether or an alkene; all of these are neutral covalent species too.

Only the reaction with sodium yields an ionic organic product.

[Textbook misprint: the book prints the last word of this question as "follwoing". It is a spelling slip for "following" and is preserved exactly as printed. The question and its answer are unaffected.]

Oxidation of an alcohol to a carbonyl compound requires a hydrogen atom on the carbon carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\). A **tertiary** alcohol has no such hydrogen, which is why the chapter states that tertiary alcohols are difficult to oxidise — they react only with strong oxidising agents at high temperature, and then by breaking \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bonds.

Classifying the four: \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH}\) is primary; \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-OH}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-CH(CH_3)-OH}\) are both secondary (the carbinol carbon carries two alkyl groups and one H); \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\) is the only one whose carbinol carbon carries three alkyl groups and no hydrogen.

The primary alcohol oxidises readily to an aldehyde and on to a carboxylic acid, and both secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones. Hence \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\) is the most resistant towards oxidation.

Resorcinol is benzene-1,3-diol, a dihydric phenol. The chapter's reduction of phenols is heating with zinc dust, which removes the phenolic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) as ZnO and reduces the ring compound to the parent arene:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{Zn} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{ZnO}\)

Applied to resorcinol both \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups are removed and nothing is added to the ring, so the product is **benzene**.

The alternatives fail on what the reagent can do. Cyclohexane would require saturation of the aromatic ring; the chapter's catalytic hydrogenation of phenol (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)/Ni, 433 K) does saturate the ring but gives cyclohexanol, and zinc dust is not a hydrogenation catalyst. Toluene would require a methyl group to be introduced, and there is no carbon source in the reaction. Benzene-1, 3-diol is resorcinol itself, i.e. no reaction at all.

Anisole is an aryl alkyl ether, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3}\). The chapter notes that in aryl alkyl ethers the bond between oxygen and the **aromatic** ring is stronger and shorter, so on reaction with HI it is the oxygen-**alkyl** bond that breaks. The aryl fragment therefore keeps the oxygen and leaves as a phenol, while the methyl group leaves as the alkyl iodide:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \xrightarrow{398\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

Methyl iodide is iodomethane, so the products are **phenol + iodomethane**.

Phenol + methanol is wrong because the alkyl group leaves bonded to iodine, not to oxygen. Iodobenzene, alone or with methanol, would require cleavage of the stronger \(\mathrm{O}\)-aryl bond, which is exactly what does not happen here.

All four compounds are phenols, so their relative acidity is set by how well the substituent stabilises or destabilises the phenoxide conjugate base.

A \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group is strongly electron-withdrawing and delocalises the negative charge of the phenoxide onto its own oxygens, stabilising it — the chapter uses precisely this to explain why p-nitrophenol is a stronger acid than phenol. So both \(\mathrm{3\text{-}NO_2-C_6H_4-OH}\) and \(\mathrm{4\text{-}NO_2-C_6H_4-OH}\) are **more** acidic than phenol itself.

A \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) group is electron-**donating** (\(+\mathrm{I}\)); it pushes electron density into the ring and destabilises the phenoxide, which is the same effect that makes an alcohol with more alkyl groups the weaker acid. So \(\mathrm{4\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-OH}\) is **less** acidic than phenol.

That leaves unsubstituted phenol lying between the methyl compound and the two nitro compounds, and \(\mathrm{4\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-OH}\) as the least acidic of the four.

Hydrogen bonding with water needs an electronegative atom in the molecule — either an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) that can donate a hydrogen bond, or an oxygen lone pair that can accept one.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\) and \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH}\) both carry \(\mathrm{-OH}\) and can both donate and accept. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O-CH_3}\) has no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), but the chapter states explicitly that ethers form hydrogen bonds with water through the ethereal oxygen, which is why their miscibility in water resembles that of alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\) is butane — a pure hydrocarbon with only \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{H}\), no electronegative atom and no lone pair. It is the one compound here incapable of hydrogen bonding with water.

Ethers combine with atmospheric oxygen on long contact with air to form peroxides, e.g.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{long contact with air}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(O-OH)-O-C_2H_5}\)

The chapter calls this a very undesirable reaction and notes that peroxides are hazardous because they decompose violently at high temperature. An air-tight bottle keeps oxygen out and a brown bottle keeps light out, so both features exist to prevent peroxide formation. Hence ethers are stored this way because they **oxidise to explosive peroxide**.

Moisture absorption is not the concern being guarded against, and a brown bottle does nothing about it. Ready evaporation is a real property of the lower ethers but is addressed by the stopper, not by the colour of the glass. Calling ethers inert contradicts the peroxide reaction itself, and if they were inert no special storage would be needed.

Ethers are neutral compounds in aqueous medium and do not react with bases, cold dilute acids, reducing agents, oxidising agents or active metals. They do, however, dissolve in **cold concentrated** \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), because the lone pair on the ethereal oxygen is protonated to give an **oxonium salt**:

\(\mathrm{R-O-R'} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-\overset{\oplus}{O}(H)-R'}\ \mathrm{HSO_4^{\ominus}}\)

This property is what distinguishes ethers from hydrocarbons.

An alkene would require dehydration, which is a reaction of alcohols and not of ethers. Alkoxides are formed when an alcohol meets an active metal such as sodium, which is a basic condition, not an acidic one. Alcohols are obtained from ethers only on hydrolysis with **hot dilute** sulphuric acid, or by cleavage with hot concentrated HI or HBr — the cold concentrated acid stops at the oxonium salt.
